title: Eighty Million Francs: the Banker Between Two Republics
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Mincing Lane, the second son
stops.date_confidence: Birth date attested, 27 October 1774: History of Parliament member 6533, the Hansard people page, and the 1885 DNB headline 'BARING, ALEXANDER, first Baron Ashburton (1774-1848)'. A 1773 variant circulates in landedfamilies.blogspot.com and on English Heritage's Northington Grange page; it does not come from the DNB, contrary to a widely copied claim. The Mincing Lane address is an inference from the family's commercial premises, not a documented birthplace.
stops.campa: The second son of Francis Baring is born in the City of London on the twenty-seventh of October, into a house that is also a countinghouse. The grandfather was Johann Baring of Bremen, a wool merchant who came ashore at Exeter and stayed; two generations on, the family trades on its own account out of Mincing Lane and lends to governments. The boy will not be given a profession to choose. He is born inside one. No source gives the room or the street of the birth. What the record keeps is the date, the parents, and the order of birth.
suggested_refs: The Baring family's Mincing Lane premises, City of London
Philip Ziegler, The Sixth Great Power, on the Exeter origins of the house

stops.name: St Gabriel Fenchurch, the parish that is only a name
stops.date_confidence: Contested and not resolved. The sole source, landedfamilies.blogspot.com, gives '25 November 1773', a year before the attested birth of 27 October 1774; the dossier silently moved it to 1774, producing a date no source states. Dated here to 1774-11-25 to hold sequence, with the conflict named. Pin corrected to the historic parish site at Fenchurch Street and Rood Lane, 51.5108, -0.0817, per Wikipedia's coordinates for St Gabriel Fenchurch.
stops.campa: A register of the united City parish records the baptism of Alexander, son of Francis Baring, on the twenty-fifth of November. The church named in the entry has not stood for over a century: St Gabriel Fenchurch burned in the Great Fire of 1666 and, alone among the ruined City churches, was never rebuilt, its parish folded into St Margaret Pattens and its ground paved over as roadway. The Barings enter their son on the books of a parish that is an address and nothing else. The one source for the entry gives the year as 1773, a year before he was born. Nobody has reconciled it.
suggested_refs: The united parish register of St Margaret Pattens with St Gabriel Fenchurch
The paved site of St Gabriel Fenchurch at the Fenchurch Street and Rood Lane junction
sources: landedfamilies.blogspot.com, '378. Baring of Grange, Barons Ashburton'

stops.name: Keizersgracht, the apprenticeship at Hope & Co
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Hope & Co.', dates his joining to 1792 and Henry Hope's flight from Hellevoetsluis to 17 October 1794, so the Amsterdam period runs c.1792-1794; the dossier's 'by around 1794' both understates and mis-dates it. Month of arrival unrecorded, defaulted to January. Pin inherited byte-identical from francis_baring.journey.json, the 1787 cochineal stop at Hope & Co's Keizersgracht 444-446 house; the coordinate is canal-belt approximate on that file's own admission.
stops.campa: At eighteen he is sent to Hope & Co on the Keizersgracht, the first issuing house in Europe, where the Dutch have made a science of lending other men's money to kings. He learns syndication, underwriting, and the bearer bond, the instrument that turns a sovereign's promise into paper any stranger can carry. Pierre César Labouchère, a partner here since 1790, will marry his sister Dorothy in 1796. On the seventeenth of October 1794 Henry Hope sails from Hellevoetsluis ahead of the French army, and the whole house moves to London.
suggested_refs: Hope & Co., Keizersgracht 444-446, Amsterdam
The removal of the Hope house to London, 1794-1795
sources: Ralph Hidy, The House of Baring in American Trade and Finance (1949), per dossier

stops.name: Philadelphia, the first resident agent
stops.date_confidence: The Baring Archive's own timeline records under 1795 'First resident agent, Alexander Baring, sent to the USA'; the dossier places the arrival in late 1795. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January. No documented street address for his Philadelphia residence was located; general city coordinates are used.
stops.campa: He lands in America at twenty-one, the family's first resident agent abroad, carrying instructions from his father to look at what the house has been lending against and to report plainly whether it is worth anything. Philadelphia is the capital, and Senator William Bingham, the richest man in it, holds two million acres of Maine on paper. Baring takes rooms in the city and learns the Willing and Bingham connection from inside it. What his father wants is a valuation, and valuations take time on the ground. He is in the country six years.
suggested_refs: The Baring Archive timeline, 1795, first resident agent in the United States
Robert C. Alberts, The Golden Voyage: The Life and Times of William Bingham (1969)
sources: Ralph Hidy, The House of Baring in American Trade and Finance (1949), per dossier

stops.name: Baring Plantation, the Penobscot to the St Croix
stops.date_confidence: Inspection tours of the Bingham tract are documented for 1796-1797; no single date or fixed point applies, the circuit covered a wide territory. Coordinate corrected to Baring Plantation, Washington County, Maine, 45.1344, -67.3156 per Wikipedia; the dossier's 45.1305, -67.4759 fell about 12 km west in unincorporated land. The 2 February 1796 memorandum to Bingham on alien landholding is folded in here: it survives, but the place of composition is unknown.
stops.campa: Between the Penobscot and the St Croix the land is standing timber with almost nobody in it. Baring rides the tract Bingham bought sight unseen, weighing what a survey, a settlement scheme, and a lumbering operation would cost against what an absentee proprietor can actually collect. In February he writes to Bingham about the disability of alien landholders under American law, a difficulty no quantity of acreage solves. Forty years later a plantation in this county will carry his name, not for the land, but for a treaty he has not yet been sent to sign.
suggested_refs: Colonial Society of Massachusetts, 'The Sale to Baring', documentary history of the Bingham Maine lands
The Baring memorandum to William Bingham, 2 February 1796, on alien landholding
sources: Colonial Society of Massachusetts, Bingham lands documentary history, per dossier

stops.name: Philadelphia, the marriage to Ann Louisa Bingham
stops.date_confidence: Date attested by Wikipedia and the DNB. landedfamilies.blogspot.com locates the ceremony 'at Blackpoint, Philadelphia', a locality this pass could not identify or geocode; central Philadelphia is used as the nearest confirmable point. The $900,000 dowry figure in circulation is an estimate and is not stated as a settlement total. francis_baring.journey.json carries a London desk-stop for the same event which says outright that the weddings happen in America and Francis is at his desk for both.
stops.campa: He marries Ann Louisa Bingham on the twenty-third of August, at a place the record calls Blackpoint and nobody since has been able to find on a map. Her father's fortune and her grandfather Thomas Willing's bank are the Federalist commercial establishment entire, and the marriage folds an English banking house into it. In London Francis Baring is at his desk, learning of the wedding by letter weeks after the fact. The dowry figure that circulates afterwards, nine hundred thousand dollars, is nobody's documented number.
suggested_refs: Robert C. Alberts, The Golden Voyage, on the Bingham and Willing connection
francis_baring.journey.json, 'Devonshire Square, the Philadelphia marriages'
sources: landedfamilies.blogspot.com, '378. Baring of Grange, Barons Ashburton'

stops.name: Devonshire Square, the return
stops.date_confidence: Return to Britain dated 1801 by the dossier's synthesis of Baring firm histories; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Pin inherited byte-identical from francis_baring.journey.json, the family house's Devonshire Square premises before the 1806 move to 8 Bishopsgate.
stops.campa: Six years in America end at a desk in Devonshire Square. He comes back with a Philadelphia wife, a working knowledge of American land titles, state debts, and the men who trade them, and a conviction he will hold to the end: that Britain and the United States have no quarrel worth a war between them. His father has built the house and his elder brother Thomas is in it. Alexander is twenty-seven and has spent six of those years on the other side of the ocean.
suggested_refs: The Baring house at Devonshire Square, London, before the 1806 move to 8 Bishopsgate
sources: Peter Austin, Baring Brothers and the Birth of Modern Finance (2007), per dossier

stops.name: Keizersgracht, Labouchere's proposal
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 30 January 1803 letter from Pierre Cesar Labouchere to Alexander Baring is known through Larry Neal's 2024 archival chapter 'Baring & Hope Anticipate Financing the Louisiana Purchase'; the primary letter was not fetched this pass. The correspondence contemplates inducements to officials on both sides but establishes no completed payment to any named recipient, and nothing more is claimed here.
stops.campa: Three months before anything is agreed in Paris, his brother-in-law writes from the Keizersgracht with a structure already drawn: Hope and Baring together will buy the American stock France is to be paid in, and place it across Europe. The letter surveys who on each side might be induced, and how. Nothing in the surviving correspondence records a payment made to any named man. Two counting houses have worked out how a continent will be paid for before the diplomats have agreed to sell it. The letter is dated the thirtieth of January 1803. The treaty is signed on the thirtieth of April.
suggested_refs: Larry Neal, 'Baring & Hope Anticipate Financing the Louisiana Purchase', in The Forgotten Financiers of the Louisiana Purchase (Palgrave Macmillan, 2024)
Northbrook Business Papers, NP1.A4, The Baring Archive
sources: The Baring Archive, 'The Louisiana Purchase' exhibition

stops.name: Paris, the bankers in the room
stops.date_confidence: The Baring Archive's Louisiana exhibition attests the Paris negotiation and its participants but gives no building and no exact day; April 1803 is the archive's own dating, defaulted here to the first of the month. General Paris coordinates are used. Where the bankers actually met Barbe-Marbois, probably the Treasury, is an open gap.
stops.campa: He crosses to Paris with Labouchère while Livingston and Monroe are still arguing over a port. The Americans have no money and no authority to borrow on this scale; the First Consul wants cash before the war resumes and cannot wait on Washington. Baring and Labouchère are the only men present who can produce the sum. Across the table is François Barbé-Marbois, Napoleon's treasury minister, who lived in Philadelphia as a young diplomat and married a Pennsylvanian, as Baring did.
suggested_refs: The Baring Archive, 'The Louisiana Purchase' online exhibition
Barbe-Marbois, Histoire de la Louisiane et de la cession de cette colonie (1829)
sources: The Baring Archive, 'The Louisiana Purchase' exhibition
napoleon.journey.json, which carries no Louisiana material at all

stops.name: Paris, the price brought down
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Baring Archive gives the reduction from 100 million francs and the settlement at 80 million francs, of which 60 million francs in United States six-percent stock. thomas_jefferson.journey.json pins this same treaty to Washington, 38.9072, -77.0369, and names no banker; the Paris pin here complements that stop rather than duplicating it.
stops.campa: France asks a hundred million francs. Baring tells the room the figure is beyond what the United States can service and beyond what any European investor will take up, and the price comes down. Treaty and claims convention are agreed at eighty million: fifteen million dollars, of which eleven and a quarter are payable not in coin but in United States six-percent stock, which Hope and Baring will buy at a discount and sell across a Europe about to go back to war. In Washington, Thomas Jefferson had authorized two million for a port.
suggested_refs: The Louisiana Purchase treaty and claims convention, 30 April 1803
thomas_jefferson.journey.json, 'Washington, Louisiana and the Corps of Discovery'
sources: The Baring Archive, 'The Louisiana Purchase' exhibition

stops.name: Washington, the letter to his father
stops.date_confidence: Attested and quoted verbatim from the letter as transcribed on the Baring Archive's Louisiana exhibition page. Coordinates mark the general Executive Mansion and Treasury vicinity of early Washington; the Treasury building of this period burned in 1814 and does not stand.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic to see the thing finished and writes to his father from Washington once the Senate's work is done. Spain has protested the cession, the Spanish flag still flies over New Orleans, and the letter is a son steadying a nervous old man in London: the trouble is delay and nothing worse. He is twenty-eight and has just underwritten a third of a continent. Sir Francis's own line on the business was that they all trembled at the magnitude of the American account.
stops.quote: The Treaty, of which I have sent you copies, has been passed without any difficulty and with little opposition
stops.quote_source: Alexander Baring to Sir Francis Baring, Washington, 21 October 1803, transcribed on The Baring Archive, 'The Louisiana Purchase' exhibition
suggested_refs: The 21 October 1803 letter, Northbrook Business Papers NP1.A4, The Baring Archive
The further lines of the same letter: 'I do not myself apprehend resistance, if it is made it must be from Havanna'
sources: The Baring Archive, 'The Louisiana Purchase' exhibition

stops.name: Devonshire Square, remittances to France forbidden
stops.date_confidence: The 16 December 1803 prohibition on Addington's order is taken from the dossier's reading of the Baring Archive's own exhibition text; the exhibition page was not independently re-fetched this pass. Britain's declaration of war in May 1803 is general historical record. The pin is the Baring house at Devonshire Square, inherited byte-identical from francis_baring.journey.json.
stops.campa: In May Britain declares war on France again, and the bond transaction becomes a question of state: money the house raises will reach Napoleon's treasury and help pay for the army massing at Boulogne. On the sixteenth of December, on Addington's order, the government formally forbids remittances to France on the Louisiana debt. It does not clearly forbid selling on the American bonds already bought. The stock is American paper, bought from the United States and not from France, and the order does not say so. Baring goes on selling it.
suggested_refs: The Addington government's prohibition of remittances to France on the Louisiana debt, 16 December 1803
sources: The Baring Archive exhibition text, as read in the dossier
Standard record of the resumption of the Napoleonic Wars, May 1803

stops.name: Washington, the first tranche
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Baring Archive's Louisiana exhibition: the first tranche of the $11.25 million in United States bonds delivered to Baring in Washington on 16 January 1804. Coordinates as for the October letter; the building itself does not survive.
stops.campa: The first tranche of the eleven and a quarter million dollars in six-percent stock is handed to him in Washington on the sixteenth of January. It is paper: engraved promises of the United States government, transferable, redeemable in fifteen years. He has bought it at a discount from a government with no other way to pay, and he will sell it in a Europe at war to men who take it because his name is on the offer. He never sees the territory it pays for, then or later.
suggested_refs: United States six-percent stock of 1803, issued to discharge the Louisiana purchase price
sources: The Baring Archive, 'The Louisiana Purchase' exhibition

stops.name: London, the prospectus in wartime
stops.date_confidence: The April 1804 London prospectus is attested through the Baring Archive's exhibition materials as read in the dossier, not re-fetched. The claim that Alexander personally compressed the remaining installment schedule for a further 1.65 million franc discount is Larry Neal's, relayed by the dossier, and is not independently confirmed. Month attested, day defaulted to the first. Pin inherited from francis_baring.journey.json, whose 'last forty million francs' stop covers the London authorization side of the same discharge.
stops.campa: Barings circulates a prospectus in the City marketing United States stock issued to pay France, while France and Britain are at war. Nobody stops it. Francis Baring authorizes it from the desk in London; Alexander is the one who has done the traveling. The subscriptions come in and the obligation to the French treasury is discharged, which is how the largest transfer of land in the hemisphere ends: with a printed sheet passed round the City. The account it opens stays in the firm's books for years.
suggested_refs: The Barings London prospectus for the American Louisiana bonds, April 1804
francis_baring.journey.json, 'Devonshire Square, the last forty million francs'
sources: The Baring Archive exhibition materials, as read in the dossier
Larry Neal, The Forgotten Financiers of the Louisiana Purchase (2024), per dossier

segments.name: The House and the House of Commons

stops.name: Threadneedle Street, a director of the Bank
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction on sourcing grounds. The 1805-1817 directorship is a standard biographical fact carried by the History of Parliament biography, but Bank of England directorial records were not re-fetched this pass. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He is elected a director of the Bank on Threadneedle Street and keeps the seat, with the customary rotations, for twelve years. He is thirty when he first takes the seat. From inside he watches the discount policy, the reserve, and the government's borrowing at close range, through the war finance, the suspension of cash payments, and the bullion controversy. Forty years later he will stand in the Lords and argue that the statute binding this Bank ought to be abrogated.
suggested_refs: Bank of England Court of Directors minutes, 1805-1817
The Bullion Report of 1810 and the debate on the suspension of cash payments
sources: History of Parliament Trust, member 6533, per dossier

stops.name: Taunton, the first seat
stops.date_confidence: Attested: MP for Taunton from November 1806 to June 1826 (Wikipedia, the DNB, History of Parliament). Day of the return not given; defaulted to the first of the month.
stops.campa: He is returned for Taunton in Somerset and will hold the seat for twenty years. He arrives in the Commons as something the House has little of: a merchant who has lived in America, speaks for the trade with it, and is willing to say in public that the war measures against neutral shipping are ruining British commerce and punishing nobody. He sits for a borough he has never lived in, on an interest bought rather than inherited, which is how most of the men around him sit.
suggested_refs: The borough of Taunton, Somerset, and its representation 1806-1826

stops.name: Devonshire Square, the house becomes Baring Brothers & Co
stops.date_confidence: Sources conflict and the conflict is not resolved here. Wikipedia's 'Barings Bank' dates the style Baring Brothers & Co from 1804, when Alexander and Henry became partners on Sir Francis's retirement; Wikipedia's Ashburton article gives 1807; the Baring Archive's own timeline carries no renaming entry at all, and francis_baring.journey.json uses 1804. Dated 1807 here only to preserve sequence. The Lawrence portrait is dated c.1810 by the Baring Archive.
stops.campa: With his father retired and his brothers Thomas and Henry beside him, the house takes the style Baring Brothers & Co, and Alexander is its working head. The premises will move to Bishopsgate. He is in his thirties and the firm is the largest merchant bank in the world. Sir Thomas Lawrence, a friend of the family, paints him about this time standing before red drapery with a hand resting on deeds, in a posture the bank's own archive would afterwards call extremely confident, perhaps even arrogant.
suggested_refs: The partnership deeds constituting Baring Brothers & Co
Sir Thomas Lawrence's portrait of Alexander Baring, c.1810, Baring family and bank collection

stops.name: The Commons, a bill of regulation and prohibition
stops.date_confidence: Attested and quoted verbatim from Hansard 1st series vol.10, Commons, 24 February 1808, 'Committee on Trade and Navigation'. The pamphlet An Inquiry into the Causes and Consequences of the Orders in Council is folded into this stop: its 1808 title and date are matters of published bibliographic record (Google Books, HathiTrust 007685511), but the text was not re-fetched and no place of composition is documented.
stops.campa: His first recorded speech in the House is against the machinery of the Orders in Council, which he tells the Commons is no bill of finance at all but a bill of regulation and prohibition that could never originate in a committee of ways and means. The same year he publishes An Inquiry into the Causes and Consequences of the Orders in Council, arguing that Britain is strangling neutral American trade for no gain and driving the United States toward war. The pamphlet is read on both sides of the water. Four years later the war comes anyway.
stops.quote: the regulations in the bill to be a complete innovation of the navigation laws. It was a bill not of finance, for the right hon. gent. could not name the amount of the duties to be expected from it; but it was a bill of regulation and prohibition, which never could originate in a committee of ways and means.
stops.quote_source: Mr. Alexander Baring, House of Commons, 'Committee on Trade and Navigation', 24 February 1808, Hansard 1st series vol.10
suggested_refs: Alexander Baring, An Inquiry into the Causes and Consequences of the Orders in Council (London, 1808), HathiTrust 007685511

stops.name: Devonshire Square, his father's death
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Sir Francis Baring died in 1810 (DNB: 'His father died in 1810'); September per the dossier, day defaulted to the first. The merger of Hope & Co's London offices into Baring Brothers in 1811 is folded into this stop and is attested by Wikipedia's Ashburton article. Pin inherited from francis_baring.journey.json.
stops.campa: Sir Francis Baring dies in September and the house is Alexander's without qualification. His elder brother Thomas has the baronetcy; Alexander has the business. The following year the London offices of Hope & Co, the Amsterdam firm that taught him the trade at eighteen, are merged into Baring Brothers: Henry Hope is dead, the Dutch house has been in exile in England since the French came, and the pupil absorbs the school. He is thirty-six years old.
suggested_refs: The absorption of Hope & Co's London offices into Baring Brothers, 1811
francis_baring.journey.json

segments.name: Rentes, a Greek House, and a Petition

stops.name: Paris, French public credit after Waterloo
stops.date_confidence: The 1817-1818 indemnity loans are documented in Oosterlinck, Ureche-Rangau and Vaslin, Journal of Economic History (2014), summarized in the dossier and not re-fetched; the article's precise meeting locations were not confirmed, so general Paris coordinates are used and the month is defaulted. The 'six great powers' saying is tradition: widely repeated, sourced by Wikipedia to Vicary Gibbs's Complete Peerage (1910), with no established first printed source or verbatim original wording.
stops.campa: France, beaten and occupied, owes an indemnity it cannot pay, and no French government can borrow at home. Baring, working with the Hopes and in steady contact with Wellington and the duc de Richelieu, converts the reparations claims into rentes and places them across Europe, restoring French public credit faster than anyone in 1815 thought possible. Richelieu is said afterwards to have named six great powers in Europe: England, France, Austria, Prussia, Russia, and Baring Brothers. Nobody has ever found the sentence in print.
suggested_refs: Oosterlinck, Ureche-Rangau and Vaslin, 'Baring, Wellington and the Resurrection of French Public Finances Following Waterloo', Journal of Economic History (2014)
Vicary Gibbs, The Complete Peerage (1910), on the 'six great powers' attribution

stops.name: The Grange, Northington: the purchase
stops.date_confidence: Purchase from Henry Drummond in 1817 attested by Wikipedia, 'The Grange, Northington'; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinate corrected to 51.1220222, -1.1989667, Wikipedia's 51 deg 7'19.28"N 1 deg 11'56.28"W; the dossier's geography lens gave 51.0989, -1.1878, about 2.7 km off and missing the house. English Heritage's history page for the site gives his birth year as 1773, following the older variant.
stops.campa: He buys The Grange at Northington from Henry Drummond, a Hampshire house that William Wilkins has been wrapping in a Greek temple, its portico not yet finished when the sale goes through. It stands five miles from Stratton Park, his father's seat. A banker who has spent twenty years turning promises into paper takes possession of a Doric temple in a Hampshire field, and then spends eight years enlarging it: a wing, then a dining room, then a conservatory eighty feet long.
suggested_refs: English Heritage, 'Northington Grange: History'
William Wilkins's Greek Revival casing of The Grange, begun for Henry Drummond

stops.name: The Commons, the London Merchants' Petition
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the exact sitting, upgrading the dossier's bare '1820': Hansard, Commons, 8 May 1820, 'COMMERCIAL RESTRICTIONS - PETITION OF THE MERCHANTS OF LONDON', cols 165-974, which opens with Baring's own words. Thomas Tooke's authorship of the petition is from free-trade historiography and was not re-fetched.
stops.campa: He rises on the eighth of May to present a petition from the merchants of London, drafted by Thomas Tooke, which states in plain terms that commercial restriction is a loss to the country that imposes it. He has the honour to rise, he tells the House, for the purpose of presenting from a most extensive and respectable body. The case for free trade is made here by the men who actually trade rather than by economists, and the Commons turns toward it over the next decade. Twenty-three years later, in the Lords, he will defend the Corn Laws.
stops.quote: Mr. Baring said, he had the honour to rise for the purpose of presenting from a most extensive and respectable body, the merchants of London.
stops.quote_source: Hansard, House of Commons, 'Commercial Restrictions - Petition of the Merchants of London', 8 May 1820, cols 165-974
suggested_refs: The London Merchants' Petition of 1820, drafted by Thomas Tooke
Stanley Chapman, The Rise of Merchant Banking (1984)
sources: Stanley Chapman, The Rise of Merchant Banking (1984), per dossier

stops.name: Bath House, Piccadilly
stops.date_confidence: Purchase in 1821 attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's 51.506558, -0.143524 for Bath House, Piccadilly; the dossier's 51.5049, -0.1469 sat about 300 m southwest, inside Green Park. Gustav Friedrich Waagen's admiration of the collection is reported by landedfamilies and was not re-fetched.
stops.campa: He buys Bath House at 82 Piccadilly and hangs it with Old Masters. The house is a working instrument as much as a residence: the collection is how a merchant's grandson signals what he is to men who inherited what he has bought. Ministers dine here, and so, later, do American envoys. Gustav Friedrich Waagen, the Berlin connoisseur who tours the English private collections, will catalogue these walls with the attention he gives to a public gallery.
suggested_refs: Gustav Friedrich Waagen, Treasures of Art in Great Britain, on the Ashburton collection at Bath House
Bath House, 82 Piccadilly, demolished 1963
sources: landedfamilies.blogspot.com, '378. Baring of Grange, Barons Ashburton'

stops.name: The Grange, the conservatory settled
stops.date_confidence: Corrected. The dossier's 'January 1823' is unsupported: Wikipedia says the Cockerell design was concluded by June 1823, with construction beginning the following March, i.e. 1824; English Heritage dates the Cockerell west-wing work, conservatory and dining room, to 1823-25. Dimensions, approximately 80 by 50 feet with an Ionic portico, are confirmed. The 6 November 1819 Jones & Clark commission for the walled kitchen garden and Robert Smirke's 1820 single-storey west wing are folded in here, both attested.
stops.campa: Charles Robert Cockerell settles the design of a conservatory for the west end of the house by June: eighty feet by fifty, fronted with an Ionic portico, iron and glass on a scale no private house in the kingdom has attempted. Building begins the following March. Jones & Clark of Birmingham, who supplied the metalwork for the walled kitchen garden four years earlier, will call the finished thing unsurpassed of its kind in the United Kingdom. Robert Smirke's plainer west wing of 1820 vanishes inside it.
suggested_refs: Charles Robert Cockerell's conservatory and dining room at The Grange, 1823-25
The Jones & Clark of Birmingham commission for the walled kitchen garden, 6 November 1819

stops.name: Bishopsgate, the loan to Buenos Aires
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and flagged. Barings' own corporate history records the 1824 Buenos Aires issue, the first external bond issue for Buenos Aires and for the country that became Argentina, but no source places Alexander Baring personally in the negotiation beyond his leadership of the house, and none places him anywhere near the Rio de la Plata. This is deliberately a London stop, not a Buenos Aires one. Month unrecorded. The discount at which the bonds were placed is standard in the literature but not verified against house papers this pass.
stops.campa: The new republic on the Rio de la Plata wants a million pounds and has credit nowhere. Baring Brothers issues the bonds in London, the first external loan of Buenos Aires and of the country it is becoming, at a price that leaves the borrower a good deal less than the face amount and the house its commission. Alexander Baring never goes near the river; the whole thing is done on paper, between Bishopsgate and a set of agents. Argentina will still be arguing about this debt a century afterwards.
suggested_refs: The 1824 Baring loan to the Province of Buenos Aires, first external bond issue of the future Argentine state
Barings corporate history, barings.com, 'Our History'
sources: Noted as a firm-level connection with no personal travel attested

stops.name: The Commons, against Buxton's motion
stops.date_confidence: The sitting and his position are attested by the separately printed speech, Mr. Alexander Baring's Speech in the House of Commons, on the 15th Day of May, 1823 (London, 1823); the Hansard record itself was not re-fetched this pass. He is not recorded as a colonial proprietor; the firm's West Indian exposure was through mortgages and advances.
stops.campa: On Thomas Fowell Buxton's motion for the abolition of slavery in the British colonies, Baring rises against Buxton and Wilberforce and accuses them of exaggerating conditions in the West Indies. He argues for gradual change managed by the colonial legislatures themselves rather than by Parliament, and against emancipation now. The speech is printed and sold separately. He is not a planter and holds no estate in the islands. He is the banker to men who do, and their debts are secured on their people.
suggested_refs: Mr. Alexander Baring's Speech in the House of Commons, on the 15th Day of May, 1823 (London, 1823)
University College London, Legacies of British Slave-ownership, on Baring firm plantation mortgages and enslaved collateral
sources: The separately printed speech of 15 May 1823, per dossier bibliography
Hansard record not re-fetched this pass

stops.name: The Commons, the memorial from Antigua
stops.date_confidence: Corrected. The dossier's chronology merged two separate sittings under 20 April 1826; Hansard, Commons, 14 April 1826, 'SLAVERY IN ANTIGUA - MEMORIAL OF COUNCIL AND HOUSE OF ASSEMBLY' is the Antigua half, with Baring's own words as quoted. He never travelled to Antigua or to any West Indian colony; this is a London stop.
stops.campa: He begs leave, he tells the House, to claim its attention to a petition of very considerable importance. It is the memorial of the council and house of assembly of Antigua against parliamentary interference with colonial slavery, and he says openly that he has no connection with the island and that the paper was simply placed in his hands. What the memorial asks is that Parliament leave the colonial legislatures to manage the question themselves. It was placed in his hands by an interest that had its choice of members.
stops.quote: begged leave to claim the attention of the House to a petition of very considerable importance
stops.quote_source: Mr. Baring, House of Commons, 'Slavery in Antigua - Memorial of Council and House of Assembly', 14 April 1826, Hansard
suggested_refs: The memorial of the council and house of assembly of Antigua, presented 14 April 1826

stops.name: The Commons, moderate and well-digested measures
stops.date_confidence: Attested and quoted verbatim: Hansard, Commons, 20 April 1826, 'PETITION OF WEST-INDIA MERCHANTS FOR PROTECTION OF THEIR PROPERTY'. This is the sitting the dossier's chronology conflated with the Antigua memorial of six days earlier; the dossier's geography lens had the two dates right.
stops.campa: Six days later he presents the London West India merchants' own petition for the protection of their property, and gives the House its formula: by gradual approaches, by moderate and well-digested measures, preparatory in their nature, and carried into execution under the guiding hand of wisdom and discretion. The merchants who sign the petition bank with him: the firm's West Indian exposure runs through mortgages and advances secured on estates. The property whose protection is asked for is people. What the sentence asks for is delay.
stops.quote: by gradual approaches, by moderate and well-digested measures, preparatory in their nature, and carried into execution under the guiding hand of wisdom and discretion.
stops.quote_source: Mr. Baring, House of Commons, 'Petition of West-India Merchants for Protection of their Property', 20 April 1826, Hansard
suggested_refs: The petition of the London West India merchants for the protection of their property, 20 April 1826

stops.name: The Commons, capital and foreign sugar
stops.date_confidence: The April 1831 argument is attested through the dossier's account of the Hansard record, not re-fetched; day given as 15 April in the dossier's geography lens and used here. His 1828 rejection of the abolitionist denial of a property right in enslaved people is folded in from the same source and carries the same reservation.
stops.campa: He tells the Commons in April that immediate emancipation would destroy British capital in the West Indies and force the country to buy its sugar from foreign slaveholders instead, so that abolition would relocate the suffering rather than end it. Three years earlier he had rejected the abolitionists' premise outright and defended the property right in an enslaved person as a right like any other. He says these things repeatedly between 1823 and 1831, to a House that is moving the other way.
suggested_refs: University College London, Legacies of British Slave-ownership, on Baring firm mortgages, enslaved collateral, and compensation interests
Slavery Abolition Act 1833 and the compensation awards to British creditors
sources: Hansard record, April 1831, per dossier account, not re-fetched

stops.name: Callington, a borough in a patron's gift
stops.date_confidence: Attested: MP for Callington, Cornwall, June 1826 to July 1831 (History of Parliament, per dossier). Day of the return not given, defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: Taunton is given up and he takes Callington in Cornwall, a borough of a few dozen electors in a patron's gift, which contemporaries call rotten without embarrassment because everybody's is. He holds it five years. The arrangement suits a man whose working hours belong to Bishopsgate: no canvass, no county interest to nurse, a seat that costs money rather than attention. It is exactly the arrangement he will spend 1831 and 1832 defending against Grey's bill.
suggested_refs: The borough of Callington, Cornwall, disfranchised by the Reform Act 1832
sources: History of Parliament Trust, per dossier

stops.name: Bloomsbury, a trustee of the British Museum
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction on sourcing grounds: British Museum trustee records were not re-fetched, and the National Gallery's own trustee page returned an access error this pass. The 1835 National Gallery trusteeship, held to his death, and his place on the Fine Arts Commission and in Partridge's group portrait are folded into this stop from the same dossier material. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He is made a trustee of the British Museum, and in 1835 one of the National Gallery, which he remains until he dies. He sits on the Fine Arts Commission and appears in John Partridge's group portrait of the commissioners, among architects and academicians and connoisseurs, one of the few men in the picture who is there for what he owns and lends rather than for anything he knows. The commission is to settle how the new Palace of Westminster will be decorated. The pictures at Bath House are the qualification.
suggested_refs: John Partridge, group portrait of the Fine Arts Commissioners, National Portrait Gallery
National Gallery, 'Alexander Baring, 1st Baron Ashburton'
sources: National Portrait Gallery record mp00151, per dossier

stops.name: Thetford, the borough and Buckenham Tofts
stops.date_confidence: Attested: MP for Thetford, Norfolk, May 1831 to December 1832 (History of Parliament, per dossier); day not given, defaulted to the first. Buckenham Tofts is folded in: the estate passed to him from William Petre, 11th Baron Petre, about 1821-22, stayed with the Barings until Lady Ashburton sold in 1869, and the hall was demolished in 1946 after Stanford Battle Area damage. Its own coordinate, 52.5203, 0.7075, is about 1.8 km west of the value the dossier carried.
stops.campa: He is returned for Thetford, another small borough, the interest attached to Buckenham Tofts, the Norfolk estate he took from Lord Petre around 1821. From this seat he opposes the Reform Bill through eighteen months of crisis, arguing against the destruction of exactly the kind of seat he is sitting in. The Barings hold Buckenham until 1869. The hall comes down in 1946, after the army takes the parish for a battle training area and empties the village around it.

stops.name: Westminster, the Exchequer that was never held
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. That he agreed in principle, after hesitation, to take the Exchequer under Wellington during the Days of May rests on standard political histories of the Reform crisis, not re-fetched; the UK Government's 'Past Chancellors' list confirms only that he never held the office. The anecdote about facing a thousand devils rather than the reformed Commons is unverified and is not repeated. His return for North Essex in December 1832, his last Commons seat, is folded in; the county division has no anchoring town.
stops.campa: With the King's government broken over the Reform Bill and Wellington trying to assemble a ministry from the wreckage, Baring is asked to take the Exchequer. He hesitates, then agrees in principle. Wellington cannot find the men, the Whigs come back, the bill passes, and the offer evaporates; his name appears on no list of Chancellors. In December he is returned for North Essex, a division the Act he fought had created, and serves his last two years in the Commons as a county member. Whether he would have taken the Exchequer had Wellington found his men is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Days of May, 1832, and Wellington's failed attempt to form a ministry
The North Essex division, created by the Reform Act 1832
sources: Standard political histories of the Reform crisis, per dossier
History of Parliament Trust, per dossier

stops.name: Whitehall, President of the Board of Trade
stops.date_confidence: Attested: President of the Board of Trade, 15 December 1834 to 8 April 1835 (Wikipedia infobox; Hansard's member record gives 'President of the Board of Trade 1834-1835'). The dossier's chronology used this one date to cover both this office and the Mint, which has its own separate start date of 23 December.
stops.campa: Peel forms his first ministry in December and gives him the Board of Trade. The man who presented the merchants' free-trade petition of 1820 now holds the office that administers the restrictions, for a hundred and fifteen days. Very little comes of it. Peel is still travelling home from Rome when the ministry is put together, and it is a minority from the hour it takes office. It falls in April. It is the first office Baring has held under the Crown, and he is sixty.
suggested_refs: Peel's first ministry, December 1834 to April 1835

stops.name: Tower Hill, Master of the Mint
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Master of the Mint, 23 December 1834 to 8 April 1835 (Wikipedia infobox). A separate appointment eight days after the Board of Trade, which the dossier's single 1834-12-15 date obscured.
stops.campa: Eight days after the Board of Trade he is given the Mint as well, an office by then largely honorary and worth holding for the salary and the standing. The Mint stands on Tower Hill, a few hundred yards from the Mincing Lane of his childhood. He runs both offices until April. The coinage is not his subject. The currency will be, thirteen years from now, when he stands in the Lords arguing that the Bank's issue of notes has been bound down by a cast-iron rule.
suggested_refs: The Royal Mint on Tower Hill, and the mastership as a ministerial office

stops.name: The House of Lords, created Baron Ashburton
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Wikipedia and the DNB: raised to the peerage as Baron Ashburton by letters patent, 10 April 1835, on the fall of Peel's ministry. The title had been held by John Dunning, dead 1783, to whom the family was connected by marriage.
stops.campa: Peel's ministry falls on the eighth of April, and on the tenth Alexander Baring is created Baron Ashburton by letters patent. He takes the title of an earlier Baron Ashburton, John Dunning the lawyer, dead since 1783, to whom the family is connected by marriage: a borrowed name, legally vacant, picked up at the fall of a government that lasted four months. The grandson of a Bremen wool merchant enters the House of Lords, and his Philadelphia wife becomes Lady Ashburton. He has not run the firm day to day for five years. He is sixty.
suggested_refs: The letters patent of 10 April 1835 creating the barony of Ashburton
John Dunning, 1st Baron Ashburton (d. 1783), and the earlier creation

stops.name: Alverstoke, the house on the Solent
stops.date_confidence: Corrected. Bay House was not acquired but built new for him in 1838 by Decimus Burton. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's 50.7867, -1.1647; the dossier's 50.7889, -1.1435 sat about 1.5 km east. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Ann Louisa's death on 5 December 1848 is confirmed by landedfamilies, but that source does not say she died here, and her death is her own stop in any case.
stops.campa: Decimus Burton builds him a seaside villa at Alverstoke on the Solent, looking across the water toward the Isle of Wight. Burton has already given London the Athenaeum and the screen at Hyde Park Corner; this is a house for an old man with money and no more offices, and he is finished with neither. In 1870, twenty-two years after his death, the Admiralty will take it on lease as a naval college and call it Ashburton House, the second building to carry that name for him.
suggested_refs: Bay House, Alverstoke, built by Decimus Burton, 1838; leased by the Admiralty in 1870 as Ashburton House
sources: landedfamilies.blogspot.com, '378. Baring of Grange, Barons Ashburton'

segments.name: The Washington Mission and the Return to the Lords

stops.name: Lafayette Square, the house Webster rented
stops.date_confidence: Arrival on 4 April 1842 attested by the US State Department, Office of the Historian: 'Lord Ashburton arrived in Washington at the head of a special mission to the United States.' Corrected against the dossier: the negotiation ran four months, 4 April to 9 August 1842, not the 'roughly ten months' Wikipedia states, which cannot be reconciled with its own arrival and signing dates and presumably counts from the mission's announcement in late 1841. The house at 1525 H Street NW was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1973 for this residency.
stops.campa: He arrives in Washington on the fourth of April as minister plenipotentiary, sixty-seven years old, sent because he is the one Englishman the Americans will trust: a man with an American wife, American children, and forty years of American accounts. Daniel Webster rents him a house on Lafayette Square across from the President's. They negotiate there rather than at the State Department, through the summer heat, with the Maine boundary, extradition, the Caroline, and the African slave trade all on one table.
suggested_refs: Ashburton House, 1525 H Street NW, Washington, National Historic Landmark, 1973
George Peter Alexander Healy's portrait of Lord Ashburton, 1842 or 1843, painted during the mission
sources: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'The Webster-Ashburton Treaty, 1842'

stops.name: Washington, the treaty signed with Webster
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The Oregon boundary was left unsettled; impressment and the Creole case were handled by understanding rather than by treaty article. Baring Plantation and Alexander, Maine are named for him as the treaty's negotiator, per Wikipedia, not for the 1790s Bingham land operation; neither town is given a stop here, a commemorative place-name being nobody's journey.
stops.campa: Four months after landing, he and Daniel Webster sign. The Maine and New Brunswick line is drawn by compromise, splitting the disputed territory; extradition is provided for; each power undertakes to keep a squadron on the African coast against the slave trade. Oregon is left where it stood. Impressment and the Creole are settled by understanding rather than by any article, which is to say not settled. Palmerston will call it the Ashburton capitulation. A plantation in Washington County, Maine is named for him.
suggested_refs: The Webster-Ashburton Treaty text, Yale Avalon Project, avalon.law.yale.edu
Wikipedia, 'Baring, Maine' and 'Alexander, Maine', both named for the treaty's negotiator
sources: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'The Webster-Ashburton Treaty, 1842'

stops.name: The Lords, the distress of the country
stops.date_confidence: Attested and quoted verbatim from Hansard 3rd series vol.66, Lords, 9 February 1843, 'Distress of the Country'. A pronoun in the dossier's version is corrected: Hansard reads 'and they owed it to the protection of the law that we were not deluged with wheat from abroad', not 'we owed it'.
stops.campa: In February he speaks in the Lords on the distress of the country and defends the Corn Laws, saying that they owed it to the protection of the law that we were not deluged with wheat from abroad. He was no bigot, he adds, but he had always thought that those general principles must be modified by the circumstances and condition of the country. It is twenty-three years since he stood in the Commons and presented the merchants' petition against commercial restriction.
stops.quote: he was no bigot, but he had always thought that those general principles must be modified by the circumstances and condition of the country.
stops.quote_source: Lord Ashburton, House of Lords, 'Distress of the Country', 9 February 1843, Hansard 3rd series vol.66
suggested_refs: Hansard 3rd series vol.66, Lords, 9 February 1843, 'Distress of the Country'

stops.name: The Lords, the Treaty of Washington defended
stops.date_confidence: Attested and quoted verbatim from Hansard 3rd series vol.68, Lords, 3 April 1843, 'Treaty of Washington'. That the Lords voted thanks on 11 April and the Commons followed after partisan debate comes from the dossier's account of the parliamentary record and was not re-fetched.
stops.campa: The treaty comes before the Lords and Ashburton defends it. He tells the House he left that country with the entire conviction that the ground taken by his noble friend was perfectly satisfactory. Aberdeen's government stands behind him. Palmerston and the opposition press the charge that he gave away the Maine boundary for the sake of a quiet mission and a comfortable summer. On the eleventh the Lords vote him their thanks. The Commons follow later, after a partisan debate.
stops.quote: I left that country with the entire conviction, that the ground taken by my noble Friend was perfectly satisfactory.
stops.quote_source: Lord Ashburton, House of Lords, 'Treaty of Washington', 3 April 1843, Hansard 3rd series vol.68
suggested_refs: Hansard 3rd series vol.68, Lords, 3 April 1843, 'Treaty of Washington'
The parliamentary votes of thanks for the Ashburton mission, April and May 1843

stops.name: The Lords, on slavery and slave trading
stops.date_confidence: Attested from Hansard 3rd series vol.68, Lords, 11 April 1843, 'Slavery and Slave Trading'. The speech is printed in Hansard's indirect third-person style, standard for the period; the quotation reproduces the printed record's own phrasing rather than his spoken words.
stops.campa: On the same day the Lords vote him their thanks for the mission, he speaks to the article binding both powers to keep squadrons against the slave trade. He assured their Lordships, the record has it, that there was no part of America which did not seriously and earnestly desire the suppression of the slave-trade. Seventeen years earlier he had presented the West India merchants' petition for the protection of their property in the Commons. Hansard prints him in the third person, as it prints everybody.
stops.quote: He assured their Lordships that there was no part of America which did not seriously and earnestly desire the suppression of the slave-trade.
stops.quote_source: Lord Ashburton, House of Lords, 'Slavery and Slave Trading', 11 April 1843, Hansard 3rd series vol.68, reported in indirect speech

stops.name: London, The Financial and Commercial Crisis Considered
stops.date_confidence: Title, publisher and year are attested bibliographic record, and the quoted passages are taken from the digitised first edition at archive.org/details/financialcommerc00ashbrich, pp. 8 and 27. Month of publication unrecorded, defaulted to January. The German edition, Beleuchtung der jetzigen finanziellen und commerciellen Krisis, said to have been printed by J. G. Cotta at Stuttgart and Tubingen the same year, could not be confirmed against any reachable library catalogue this pass.
stops.campa: At seventy-two he publishes forty pages with John Murray against the Bank Charter Act of 1844, in the middle of a commercial panic he says the Act has made worse. The passage from ample, perhaps profuse Bank accommodation to severe restriction had produced in both years, and ever will produce, the same symptoms. An adverse state of the foreign exchanges, he writes, is to be corrected by making money scarce. It runs to at least three English editions. A German edition is said to have been printed at Stuttgart the same year, though no library catalogue confirms one.
stops.quote: The passage from ample, perhaps profuse Bank accommodation to severe restriction had produced in both years, and ever will produce, the same symptoms
stops.quote_source: Alexander Baring, Lord Ashburton, The Financial and Commercial Crisis Considered (London: John Murray, 1847), p.8

stops.name: The Lords, the cast-iron rule
stops.date_confidence: Attested and quoted verbatim from Hansard 3rd series vol.95, Lords, 2 December 1847, 'The Currency: Commercial Distress'. This is his last recorded intervention of substance; he dies five months later.
stops.campa: In December, with the panic at its height, he tells the Lords that the cast-iron rule which bound down the Bank in its issue of notes ought to be abrogated, and that a discretionary power ought to be given to the Directors, since twenty millions might be dangerous at one time and twenty-five perfectly safe at another. He would earnestly advise, he says, that the suspension of the restrictive clauses take place immediately. He sat as a director of that Bank for twelve years, before any such rule existed.
stops.quote: The cast-iron rule which bound down the Bank in its issue of notes ought to be abrogated. A discretionary power ought to be given to the Directors, for it was well known that while an issue of twenty millions might be dangerous at one time, twenty-five millions might be perfectly safe at another.
stops.quote_source: Lord Ashburton, House of Lords, 'The Currency: Commercial Distress', 2 December 1847, Hansard 3rd series vol.95
suggested_refs: Hansard 3rd series vol.95, Lords, 2 December 1847, 'The Currency: Commercial Distress'

stops.name: Longleat, the end
stops.date_confidence: Date contested and not reconciled: Hansard's member record and History of Parliament give 12 May 1848; the 1885 DNB gives 13 May. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's 51.1857, -2.2743 for Longleat House; the dossier's two lenses gave 51.1653, -2.1965 and 51.1969, -2.1897, both roughly 6 km out and in different directions. No source consulted gives a cause of death. The burial place is a genuine gap: the DNB names none, and the dossier's own geography lens and afterlife lens contradict each other on whether he lies at Northington, so no burial stop is written.
stops.campa: He dies at Longleat in Wiltshire, in his son-in-law's family's house, five months after his last speech on the currency, aged seventy-three. Lansdowne, Brougham, and Derby speak of him in the Lords. He leaves five sons and four daughters, a barony, The Grange, Bath House, the villa on the Solent, and a bank. No source names the place of his burial. His widow Ann Louisa, the senator's daughter he married in Philadelphia fifty years before, outlives him by seven months.
